title: My first game in almost 20 years, using Fable and Astra: the cache and balance problems behind it
author: Baytelman
selftext:
I made Monkeys Go Bananas, my first game in almost 20 years. It’s a funny alternative to Polytopia—think pocket-sized Civilization, with monkeys. I developed it using Fable and Astra, and wanted to share some of the less glamorous work behind getting it onto phones.

The stack is TypeScript game logic, React UI, Canvas2D rendering and a Capacitor iOS shell. A Unity rewrite was considered and deferred because it would mean throwing away the existing TypeScript work. Godot was left as something to evaluate alongside Unity if an engine switch becomes necessary. PixiJS was an early rendering candidate; the game ended up using plain Canvas2D.

Performance was a much bigger challenge than the small board suggested. One slowdown involved sprite identities and zoom values making a raster cache miss repeatedly. Even a still board could redraw expensive shapes instead of reusing them. The useful fix was to address what made the cache miss, rather than just redraw less often. An early-board probe also missed the conditions that appeared later in a match, so the test scene mattered as much as the proposed optimisation.

Balance has a different trap. The rules are deterministic, so seeded computer-versus-computer games let the same scenarios be repeated after a change. That helps expose economy and opponent skew. It doesn’t tell me whether a human understands the next move or wants another game. I’m trying to keep those questions separate: automated matches for rule changes, actual players for clarity and enjoyment.

That’s the part of AI-assisted development I’d like to compare notes on: what do you use to check that a plausible fix solved the real problem? In this project, reproducible game states and tests that reach the failure have mattered a lot.

If seeing the game helps give context: https://monkeysgo.app has browser play and the iPhone App Store link.
